about: Field studies of heat strain in Asian agricultural and salt work, found through Europe PMC (November 2026) to answer the cotton page's first gap: nobody has yet measured heat strain among cotton workers in Asia. None of these studies is about cotton. Each claim rests on the exact words of a study abstract; stage.js stages them, verify-sources.yml checks them, gate.js keeps only what passed. Searched: heat strain, core or body temperature, heart rate, WBGT, urine specific gravity, heat-related illness and kidney markers among farmers, farmworkers and agricultural, rice, sugarcane, tea, salt and brick workers in South and Southeast Asian countries, 2008-2026, plus intervention terms (rest breaks, shade, hydration, trial).

claims.text: In rice fields in West Bengal, India, hourly heat (WBGT) was 26-32°C. Among 124 harvesters, most reported exhaustion and pain on hot days; in 48 whose heart rate was recorded, it recovered more slowly at high heat, and bundles collected fell by about 5% for each degree of WBGT above 26°C.
rests_on: Heart rate recovered quickly at low heat, but more slowly at high heat

claims.text: In a small study of 14 people transplanting paddy by hand in Northeast India, oral temperature rose by 0.5°C after 65 minutes of work at the lower heat levels studied. The authors propose work-rest cycles that shorten as heat rises, down to 35 minutes of work and 22 of rest at a WBGT of 31-32°C.
Among 200 men harvesting paddy in West Bengal from April to June 2024, heat (WBGT) predicted physiological strain hour by hour; older age added to the strain and work experience was protective.

claims.where: Field and brick work; salt and water
claims.text: Among agricultural and brick-field workers in eastern India, sweat gland activity was higher in summer. Blood electrolytes stayed in the normal range at the monitoring sessions, but full-shift heat above a WBGT of about 23-25°C was associated with a higher probability of low blood sodium.
rests_on: Sweat gland activation was also significantly higher during the summer season

claims.text: Among 379 rice farmers in Ha Tinh province, Viet Nam, 83.4% reported at least one heat-related symptom during the 2021 summer-autumn harvest. More than 4 hours outdoors in the heat and heavy tasks were associated with more illness, and drinking more water with less.

In the hottest month of a Thai sugarcane harvest, cane cutters faced high heat stress and strain, with dehydration and rises in heart rate and body temperature across the shift; workers in the sugar factory were at low risk.
rests_on: Dehydration was observed among sugarcane cutters

claims.text: In Nakhon Sawan, Thailand, sugarcane harvesters' heat stress exceeded the occupational limit (ACGIH) for 72.7% of working time in the cooler months and 90.9% in the hotter month; harvesting burnt cane added to the heat.
rests_on: harvesting burnt sugarcane were significantly associated with increased effective WBGT

claims.text: Among 295 Thai sugarcane workers (165 men, 130 women), 98% reported at least one heat-related symptom and 74% at least one severe symptom. Symptoms rose with each degree of full-shift heat, and the study found no significant difference in risk between women and men.
Among 287 Thai sugarcane workers, each degree of full-shift heat was associated with about 9 fewer stalks harvested per hour.

Among 200 sugarcane farmers in Kamphaeng Phet, Thailand, 48% reported heat-related illness symptoms in summer. Being a woman and wearing two-layer shirts were associated with higher risk, and drinking 3.1-5.0 litres a day with lower risk.
rests_on: The prevalence of heat-related illness symptoms was 48%

claims.text: Thai sugarcane cutters and farmers, most of them women, both had higher urinary markers of kidney injury after the shift than before, more so among cutters. Cutters exceeded recommended heat exposure; farmers did not.
rests_on: 62% of cutters and 56% of farmers were female
cross-shift changes of NGAL were significantly higher for sugarcane cutters

claims.text: Over six months in Malaysia, conventional farmworkers adapted less well to heat than agroecological farmers; the authors link this to earlier metabolic effects of pesticide exposure.

In seven Indian salt pans, where there is no pesticide exposure, 87% of 352 workers exceeded the heat-stress limit and median water intake over the workday was one litre. Workers above the limit had 2.9 times the odds of reduced kidney function.
rests_on: absence of occupational exposures to pesticides

claims.text: Among 50 sea salt workers in Thailand, more than half were dehydrated after work.
rests_on: more than 50% of the participants were dehydrated after work

claims.text: In chronic kidney disease hotspot villages of Bargarh district, Odisha, screening of 1,136 people identified 157 potential cases of heat stress nephropathy, 63.3% of them farmers. The study is cross-sectional and does not show cause.
rests_on: 157 potential cases of heat stress nephropathy

claims.text: Among 261 agricultural workers in four villages of Sri Lanka's North Central Province, a heat stress and dehydration symptom index was not associated with urine albumin or urine concentration; the authors note that urine albumin is not a reliable marker of early disease.
rests_on: heat stress-dehydration index overall was not associated with ACR
not a reliable marker of early CKDu

claims.text: Across 11 districts of Tamil Nadu, WBGT measured at outdoor workplaces exceeded 30°C, and among 1,560 informal outdoor workers higher heat was associated with 1.4 times the risk of reported productivity loss.

A 2026 mapping review of 210 field reports from low- and middle-income countries found 40% from the South-East Asia Region and 30% from India; agriculture made up 33%. 39% of reports included no women, and only 9% included any intervention to protect workers.
rests_on: 39% of reports not including any female participants
only 9% included some form of intervention
